analysis.one_liner: Lets antitrust laws apply to health insurers, banning price fixing among them.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote: it died in the House Judiciary Committee with zero cosponsors after being referred to a subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill strips health insurers and medical malpractice insurers of a special legal shield they hold under the McCarran-Ferguson Act, a 1945 law that exempts the insurance industry from most federal antitrust rules. Without that shield, insurers could be sued and prosecuted for price fixing, bid rigging, and dividing up markets, the same as most other industries. The bill never moved beyond a referral to a House subcommittee and received no cosponsors.
analysis.who_benefits: People and employers who buy health insurance. Exposing insurers to antitrust law would let regulators and private lawsuits challenge collusion among insurers, which can push premiums higher and has been cited in past cases involving malpractice insurers and insurance trade groups sharing competitively sensitive data.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the industry-wide exemption from federal antitrust laws for health insurers and medical malpractice insurers, so price fixing, bid rigging, and market allocation are clearly illegal for them [S2][S3].

Makes unfair methods of competition rules apply to health insurers regardless of whether they operate for profit, closing a loophole that could otherwise let nonprofit insurers escape enforcement [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurance and medical malpractice insurance companies, which could no longer engage in or shield from scrutiny practices like sharing pricing data and coordinating market behavior, and could face lawsuits and enforcement actions as a result. Insurers might pass some compliance and litigation costs to customers, which is the standard objection from the industry.

drawbacks.text: Opponents argue that state insurance regulators, not federal antitrust law, are the proper way to police the insurance business, and that the McCarran-Ferguson exemption lets regulators supervise insurers comprehensively without the unpredictability of antitrust litigation [S2].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that antitrust suits are slow and costly, that insurers' market power is driven heavily by how few competitors exist in many local markets rather than by collusion alone, and that any new litigation costs could end up partly reflected in premiums.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real, documented carve-out: health insurers are among the few businesses largely exempt from federal antitrust law. Removing it would give enforcers and patients a legal tool against collusion that currently does not exist. The main cost is legal uncertainty and possible litigation expense for insurers, which is the normal price of antitrust rules that virtually every other industry already lives under. The bigger weakness is that the bill is narrow — it does nothing to increase competition directly, only to make collusion illegal.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on the first day of the 115th Congress, referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its antitrust subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers Jr. introduced the bill on January 3, 2017, the first day of the 115th Congress [S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
On January 23, 2017, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law, where it remained [S5].
No other action was ever taken, and no cosponsors signed on in the House [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers keep their exemption from federal antitrust law, and the status quo of limited insurer competition in many markets continues.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers, who kept their antitrust exemption

for.name: Rep. John Conyers Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; found no cosponsors.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the full committee and then to its antitrust subcommittee; never held a hearing or markup.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew no cosponsors and no votes, so no partisan split is visible in the record, though similar McCarran-Ferguson repeal efforts have generally leaned Democratic.

industries.note: The bill would end their broad exemption from federal antitrust law, exposing pricing coordination and market division to lawsuits and enforcement. Their interest in keeping the exemption runs against consumers, who currently lack a federal antitrust remedy against insurer collusion.

Same exemption would be removed for malpractice insurers, which matters for doctors' premiums and, indirectly, patients' access to care. This is the first time malpractice insurers would be named under antitrust law in this way.
